title: DSA: intervals, scheduling, bit manipulation and CIDR
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Merge intervals, meeting rooms, insert interval, subnet masks and host counts, popcount, n & (n-1) and XOR tricks.
source: LeetCode Merge Intervals, Meeting Rooms I/II, Insert Interval, Single Number, Counting Bits, Missing Number, Non-overlapping Intervals; Oracle Java Tutorials (bitwise operators); JLS 15.19 shift operators; Python docs (int.bit_count); RFC 4632, RFC 3021

questions.prompt: Merge the closed intervals [1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18], [17,20]. How many intervals are in the merged result?
Meetings are [1,4], [2,5], [3,6], [7,9]. What is the minimum number of rooms needed?
questions.explanation: At time 3 the first three meetings overlap (1-4, 2-5, 3-6), so 3 rooms are required; [7,9] can reuse a freed room. The answer is the maximum overlap depth.

questions.prompt: How many usable host addresses does a /26 IPv4 subnet have (excluding network and broadcast addresses)?
questions.explanation: 32 - 26 = 6 host bits, 2^6 = 64 addresses, minus network and broadcast = 62. (A /31 point-to-point link is a special case under RFC 3021.)

questions.prompt: 1000 in binary is 1111101000. What does Integer.bitCount(1000) return?
questions.explanation: Ones in 1111101000: five in a row plus one more = 6. Brian Kernighan's n &= n - 1 loop would iterate exactly 6 times.

questions.prompt: What must you do to the interval list before the single-pass merge loop works?

options.text: Sort the intervals by start time.
options.why: Correct: then any overlap is with the last merged interval only.

options.text: Sort by end time, then compare each interval with the first one in the output.
options.why: Sorting by end does not guarantee that the last merged interval is the only possible overlap.

options.text: Build a HashSet of all start times and look up each end.
options.why: Hashing cannot express "overlaps" because it is a range relation, not equality.

options.text: Nothing, because the loop compares every pair of intervals anyway.
options.why: Comparing every pair is O(n^2) and not what the single-pass merge does.

questions.explanation: Sort by start (O(n log n)), then sweep in O(n), extending the last output interval or starting a new one.

questions.prompt: For a positive int n, what does the expression (n & (n - 1)) == 0 test?

options.text: That n is a power of two, because n has exactly one set bit.
options.why: Correct: n - 1 flips the lowest set bit and everything below it, so the AND clears only that bit.

options.text: That n is even, because the lowest bit of n is 0.
That n has exactly two set bits, one removed by the subtraction.
options.why: Two set bits leave one bit after the AND, so the result is non-zero.

options.text: That n is a multiple of 10, since n - 1 ends in 9.
options.why: Decimal reasoning does not apply to bitwise AND.

questions.explanation: Guard n > 0 because 0 & -1 == 0 would wrongly pass. The same n & (n-1) step removes the lowest set bit, which powers popcount.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method int[][] merge(int[][] iv) that merges all overlapping closed intervals (touching intervals like [1,2] and [2,3] also merge) and returns the result in sorted order.

checks.label: extends the last interval using Math.max of the ends
collects results in a list or array and returns it
treats touching intervals as overlapping (<= or not >)

questions.explanation: Copy x into a new array before adding so you do not mutate the caller's input. Prefer Integer.compare over a[0] - b[0], which can overflow with extreme values. Time O(n log n). Other valid approaches exist, e.g. keeping start and end in local variables.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function min_rooms(meetings) where meetings is a list of [start, end] pairs. Return the minimum number of rooms using a min-heap of end times. A meeting that starts exactly when another ends can reuse the room.

checks.label: sorts the meetings by start time
uses heapq push and pop on end times
frees a room when the earliest end is <= the new start

questions.explanation: The heap size at the end equals the peak number of rooms, since a room is only added when none is free. A sweep line over sorted starts and ends is an equally good O(n log n) solution. For [[0,5],[5,10]] the answer is 1 because of the <= test.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method boolean inSubnet(int ip, int network, int prefixLen) that returns true if the 32-bit IPv4 address ip belongs to the CIDR block network/prefixLen, using bit operations. Handle prefixLen == 0.
questions.starter:
static boolean inSubnet(int ip, int network, int prefixLen) {
  
}

checks.label: builds or applies a mask from 32 - prefixLen
compares the masked/xor-ed values for equality
uses a bitwise & (or ^) to apply the mask

questions.explanation: The guard matters: in Java the shift distance of an int shift is taken mod 32 (JLS 15.19), so -1 << 32 is still -1 and a /0 would wrongly demand an exact match. An alternative is (ip ^ network) >>> (32 - p) == 0 with the same guard.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function popcount(n) for n >= 0 that counts the set bits using the n & (n - 1) trick, without bin() or int.bit_count().

checks.label: clears the lowest set bit with n & (n - 1)

questions.explanation: Runs in O(number of set bits). In real code use n.bit_count() (Python 3.10+) or Integer.bitCount(n) in Java, which map to a hardware instruction. For negative Python ints bit tricks need a mask because ints are unbounded.

questions.prompt: You must insert one new interval into a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals.
questions.assertion: Insert Interval can be solved in O(n) time without sorting again.
questions.reason: The existing list is already sorted and non-overlapping, so one left-to-right pass (before, overlapping, after) is enough.

whys.a: Right: the sorted, disjoint input is what permits the single pass.
whys.b: R is the cause, not a side fact.

questions.explanation: Add intervals ending before the new one, merge all that overlap by min of starts and max of ends, then append the rest.

questions.prompt: Consider the Java expression -1 >>> 28 on an int.
questions.reason: The >>> operator sign-extends the left operand while shifting.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: -1 is 32 ones; >>> fills with zeros leaving the top 4 bits as 1111 = 15, and >>> does not sign-extend, so R is false.

questions.explanation: Use >>> to treat an int as unsigned (IP addresses!). -1 >> 28 stays -1 because >> sign-extends. Python has no >>>; its ints are unbounded, so mask with & 0xFFFFFFFF.

questions.prompt: Match each interval problem with its standard technique.

left.text: Calendar booking: does a new event collide?
Insert one interval into a sorted disjoint list

right.text: Min-heap of end times (or sweep line)
Sort by end time, pick greedily

questions.explanation: Sorting by start fits merging; heap of end times tracks rooms in use; earliest-end-first is the greedy for activity selection; TreeMap neighbours check collisions in O(log n); the sorted input lets Insert Interval run in one O(n) pass.

questions.prompt: Complete the facts about a /27 IPv4 subnet.
questions.text: A /27 has mask 255.255.255.{1}, {2} total addresses and {3} usable hosts.
questions.explanation: 27 network bits leave 5 host bits: 2^5 = 32 addresses, 30 usable. The last octet mask is 11100000 = 224. A /26 would give 64 and 62.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which XOR facts are correct?

options.why: Correct: every bit cancels with itself.
Correct: XOR with zero changes nothing.

options.text: XOR of all elements returns the value that appears once if every other value appears exactly twice.
options.why: Correct: pairs cancel to 0, leaving the single value (Single Number).

options.text: a ^ b == a + b for all non-negative a and b.
options.why: False: 3 ^ 1 = 2 but 3 + 1 = 4; they agree only when no bit position overlaps.

questions.explanation: XOR is associative and commutative, which is why the order of elements does not matter. Swapping without a temp is a party trick, not production code.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum number of intervals to remove from [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[1,3]] so that the rest do not overlap (touching at an endpoint is allowed)?
questions.explanation: Remove [1,3]; the others touch only at endpoints. The greedy sorts by end time, keeps an interval whenever it starts at or after the last kept end, and counts the rest: n minus the maximum non-overlapping set, O(n log n).

questions.prompt: In 32-bit two's complement, what is the value of 12 & -12?
questions.explanation: 12 is 1100 and -12 is ...110100, so the AND leaves only the lowest set bit, 0100 = 4. The expression n & -n isolates that bit and drives Fenwick tree indexing.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function missing_number(nums) for a list holding n distinct numbers taken from 0..n with one missing; return the missing one in O(n) time and O(1) extra space using XOR or a sum.

checks.label: uses the length of the list as n
combines values with XOR or a sum

questions.explanation: XOR of 0..n with every element cancels all pairs and leaves the missing number. n(n+1)/2 - sum(nums) is the equally valid sum version (beware overflow in Java: use long). Sorting or a hash set would use more time or space.

questions.prompt: Complete the recurrence that counts the set bits of every number from 0 to n in O(n).
questions.text: With bits[0] = {1}, use bits[i] = bits[i {2} 1] + (i {3} 1): drop the lowest bit, then add it back if it was set.
questions.explanation: This is LeetCode 338 (Counting Bits). The answer for i reuses an already computed smaller number, so it is a DP over bits; i & (i - 1) works too: bits[i] = bits[i & (i - 1)] + 1.
